title: Nat Alison- In Defense of Hand-Crafted Sudoku
speaker: Nat Alison
summary: Nat Alison, a variant sudoku constructor, argues that although sudoku is known as the ultimate procedurally generated puzzle, a thriving community (grown around the Cracking the Cryptic YouTube channel during the pandemic) prizes hand-crafted puzzles. Their appeal lies in the variety of variant rules, constructor ingenuity in creating new deductions, and the 'story' a human-designed solve path tells, with a break-in leading to a flow of deductions. Through live demos in the f-puzzles tool, she shows that hand-made puzzles can still feel procedural if tools merely resolve a doodle, while computer-searched puzzles like the Miracle Sudoku can feel hand-crafted when a human curates for a meaningful idea. She concludes handcrafted versus procedural is a spectrum and that people ultimately want to communicate with other humans.

insights.claim: Computer-generated sudoku that can all be solved with the same fixed set of algorithmic steps quickly becomes boring.
insights.detail: Alison describes newspaper and airport-book sudoku as procedural puzzles where you repeatedly apply the same row/column eliminations; she positions her talk as a counterexample to procedural sudoku generation.
insights.quote: For most of these puzzles you have a specific set of instructions and algorithms

insights.claim: The hand-crafted variant sudoku community grew rapidly from 2020 via a feedback loop in which Cracking the Cryptic videos inspired viewers to build puzzles, which got featured and inspired more constructors.
insights.detail: Alison explains the channel moved from cryptic crosswords to newspaper sudoku to hand-crafted variants; pandemic viewers sent by the algorithm became solvers and constructors, forming Discords and other channels.
insights.quote: A sort of feedback loop happened where people look at the puzzle and see the logic and people think this is cool

insights.claim: Variant sudoku gets its variety from layering rule types such as anti-knight, killer cages, thermometers, whisper lines, irregular regions, chaos construction and even fog of war that reveals clues as correct digits are placed.
insights.detail: Alison argues that while a generator can produce sextillions of classic grids, only human ingenuity has invented genuinely new rule combinations; killer cages in newspapers stayed basic for years.
insights.quote: they also added fog of war to Sudoku where the digits that you put in if they are correct reveal more fog and reveal more clues

insights.claim: Hand-crafted puzzles can contain new kinds of deductions a computer would brute-force but a human can solve logically, and constructors build a shared 'meta game' of theorems on each other's work.
insights.detail: Examples include Leapfrog, a pure killer puzzle tracking digits across rows, and Arbitrary Code Execution, which uses coloring of 7-8-9 triples. People continually devise and build upon new theorems.
insights.quote: There is a Sudoku meta game. People come up with new theorems all of the time

insights.claim: Human-designed puzzles have a story: a core 'break-in' deduction that flows through developing logic to a resolution, whereas computer-generated puzzles lack a set path.
insights.detail: Alison says every human puzzle has a story the setter wants to tell, e.g. that a seemingly impossible scenario has a solution, demonstrating a new theorem interactively, or trolling friends.
insights.quote: Puzzles by humans have a flow to them. There is a sort of break in the core thing that you want people to realize about the puzzle

insights.claim: A large community of creators building on each other's work can supply hundreds of hours of fresh play, a role procedural generation usually plays in other spaces.
insights.detail: Alison contrasts looking to procedurality for content and play time with the hand-crafted sudoku community, where people make puzzles inspired by others' puzzles.
insights.quote: You look toward the procedurality as a way to generate more content and more play time

insights.claim: Constructing a hand-crafted puzzle starts with an idea, like combining or modifying constraints, then turning the resulting break-in into themed deductions, guided by what the constructor wants to see solved.
insights.detail: Alison builds intuition by solving along with videos, then asks questions like what happens if two constraint types combine. Sometimes something breaks and the resulting logic is itself worth showing.
insights.quote: What happens if I combine these two types of constraints?

insights.claim: Constructing logic puzzles often feels like discovery rather than creation: the designer sets rules and traverses the space of possible worlds to find an interesting one, like finding a good Minecraft seed.
insights.detail: Alison describes this as co-constructing with the universe and ties it back to roguelikes.
insights.quote: sometimes is t doesn't feel like you are creating a puzzle but it feels like you are discovering it

insights.claim: Using a solver tool merely to resolve a doodled grid produces a 'hand-crafted' puzzle that still feels procedural, with no intended solve path and clues added only for uniqueness.
insights.detail: Alison live-built an '@'-shaped whisper-line sudoku in f-puzzles in two minutes, then pointed out its small X clues added nothing meaningful to the logic and it would solve like an airport newspaper puzzle.
insights.quote: It is possible to make hand-crafted puzzles that feel procedural even though I drew everything in the grid

insights.claim: Constructors use solver tools well by shortcutting bad paths and testing combinations, then working out the human logic themselves so the solver is steered to a unique, meaningful path.
insights.detail: For a chaos construction Alison used the f-puzzles tool to try final region combinations, but wrote the logic herself. In another puzzle, a solver revealed an odd parity pattern; she worked out why, found interesting logic and built the puzzle around it.
insights.quote: One way that I have seen tools use and I have used myself is the shortcutting of bad paths

insights.claim: Puzzles like the Miracle Sudoku and some by setter Clypeal are essentially computer-generated yet feel hand-crafted, because the value lies in a human discovering that such a constrained puzzle exists and curating the most beautiful solve path.
insights.detail: Alison re-creates the Miracle Sudoku in seconds with a solver, noting there are only one or two solutions up to symmetry, so the idea is that it can exist at all. Clypeal wrote a program to generate combinations and picked the one with the most beautiful solve path.
insights.quote: Ended up with like four different solutions that worked and picked the one that had the most beautiful solve path

insights.claim: Hand-crafted versus procedural is a spectrum rather than a binary; what matters is human intent and curation communicating something to other humans.
insights.detail: Alison applies this to games: people want to tell and hear stories, whether a cool theorem, a set storyline, or a wild anything-can-happen experience. She notes computer-generated 'chaff' floods the sudoku market while hand-crafted setters rely on Patreon.
insights.quote: hand-crafted verse procedural isn't a binary. It is a spectrum
